column1: af|A Buddhist crossroads|Long before its modern borders, Afghanistan was a meeting place of Buddhist artistic traditions. The Bamiyan Valley preserves monasteries and sanctuaries spanning centuries of that history.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/208/

al|One town, several civilizations|At Butrint, a walk through the ruins passes through a Greek colony, a Roman city and a bishopric. Marshes eventually helped bring this once-busy town to abandonment.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/570/

dz|The Sahara has a picture archive|Tassili n’Ajjer holds more than 15,000 prehistoric drawings and engravings. They record changing animals, people and climate in a landscape that looks very different today.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/179/

ad|A valley that takes up a country-sized slice|Andorra’s Madriu-Perafita-Claror Valley covers about 9% of the whole country. Its mountain landscape still reflects a communal land-ownership tradition dating to the 13th century.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1160/

ao|A capital built around a sacred tree|Mbanza Kongo was a capital of the Kingdom of Kongo. Its historic centre grew around a royal residence, a court and a holy tree, placing sacred and political landmarks together.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1511/

ag|A harbour designed by nature|Antigua’s deep, narrow bays and surrounding hills made a natural hurricane shelter for sailing ships. That geography helped determine where the British built their naval dockyard, using enslaved African labour.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1499/

ar|Trees older than the Roman Empire|The alerce trees protected in Los Alerces National Park belong to a species that can live for more than 3,600 years. Some Patagonian forests are living records measured in millennia.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1526/

am|Medieval book-making schools|Sanahin monastery was famous for its calligraphers and manuscript illuminators. These Armenian monasteries were centres of learning as well as places of worship.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/777/

au|An annual meeting of ocean giants|Whale sharks gather at Western Australia’s Ningaloo Coast every year. The same protected landscape also has a hidden world of underground caves and streams beneath the land.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1369/

at|A zoo in an imperial garden|Schönbrunn’s palace gardens contain the zoo founded in 1752. The grounds bring an imperial residence and an extraordinarily long zoological history into the same place.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/786/

az|A forest with a prehistoric pedigree|The Hyrcanian forests shared by Azerbaijan and Iran trace their history back 25–50 million years. They are remnants of forests that once spread much more widely across northern temperate regions.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1584/

bh|Thousands of ancient towers for the dead|Bahrain’s Dilmun heritage site includes roughly 11,774 burial mounds. Many were originally low cylindrical towers, built between about 2200 and 1750 BCE.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1542/

bd|Tiger country at the edge of the sea|The Sundarbans is a maze of tidal channels and salt-tolerant mangroves where Bengal tigers live alongside crocodiles. A tiger habitat does not have to look like an inland jungle.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/798/

bb|A city that refused the grid|Bridgetown’s historic streets curve and wind. That layout sets it apart from the orderly grids used for many Spanish and Dutch colonial cities in the Caribbean.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1376/

by|A castle made from ten buildings|Nesvizh Castle is an interconnected complex of ten buildings arranged around a six-sided courtyard. Its owners helped turn the town into a centre of art, science and craftsmanship.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1196/

be|Lifts for boats|Belgium’s historic Canal du Centre has four hydraulic boat lifts. They are the surviving examples of their era that UNESCO identifies as remaining in their original working condition.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/856/

bz|A reef on a continental scale|Belize’s coast forms part of the largest barrier reef in the Northern Hemisphere. The protected system includes not just coral, but atolls, mangroves, lagoons and hundreds of sandy cays.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/764/

bj|A last stronghold for West African lions|Benin shares the W-Arly-Pendjari protected complex with Burkina Faso and Niger. UNESCO identifies it as the home of the region’s only viable lion population.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/749/

bo|A mountain that powered an industry|In the 1500s, Potosí was an enormous silver-production centre. Artificial lakes and aqueducts supplied water to mills processing ore from Cerro Rico—the “Rich Mountain.”|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/420/

ba|A cave full of living fossils|Vjetrenica Cave shelters animals whose nearest relatives disappeared long ago. It is also home to the only known subterranean tubeworm described in UNESCO’s account of the site.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1673/

bw|An art gallery in the desert|Tsodilo holds more than 4,500 rock paintings in just 10 square kilometres of the Kalahari. The landscape records human activity stretching back at least 100,000 years.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1021/

br|Brazil has more than rainforest|The Cerrado is an ancient tropical savannah ecosystem. Its protected areas have sheltered species through past climate shifts, making this less-famous Brazilian landscape a remarkable refuge.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1035/

bg|Half-human, half-plant sculptures|Inside the ancient Thracian tomb at Sveshtari, ten carved female figures blend human and plant forms. The tomb dates to the third century BCE but was only discovered in 1982.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/359/

bf|Iron-making before the Roman Empire|At Douroula, evidence of iron production dates to the eighth century BCE. Burkina Faso’s heritage sites also preserve standing furnaces from later iron-working traditions.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1602/

kh|Cambodian temples before Angkor|Sambor Prei Kuk has more than 100 temples, including ten unusual octagonal ones. The site belonged to an earlier Khmer capital that flourished before the famous Angkor period.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1532/

cm|A river almost wraps a rainforest|The Dja River nearly encircles Cameroon’s Dja Faunal Reserve. This natural boundary surrounds a rainforest refuge with more than a hundred recorded mammal species.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/407/

ca|Tropical-sea fossils in Quebec|Anticosti Island preserves marine fossils spanning roughly ten million years around Earth’s first major animal mass extinction. Today’s Canadian island was once beneath an ancient tropical sea.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1686/

cv|An Atlantic town with an early tropical chapter|Cidade Velha, formerly Ribeira Grande, is identified by UNESCO as the first European colonial outpost in the tropics. Parts of its early street layout survive on Santiago island.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1310/

cf|A landscape that switches habitats|Manovo-Gounda St Floris combines broad savannahs with northern floodplains. That contrast makes room for very different wildlife communities, from land mammals to waterbirds.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/475/

td|Fresh water in the Sahara|Chad’s Ounianga site has 18 lakes fed by groundwater in an extremely dry desert. Some are salty, while others support freshwater fish; floating reeds help limit evaporation.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1400/

cl|A town built around a staircase|Sewell was built so high and steep in the Andes that wheeled vehicles were impractical. Its colourful mining-town buildings grew around a great central staircase instead.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1214/

cn|A rest stop for millions of birds|China’s Yellow Sea and Bohai Gulf wetlands are a bottleneck on a huge migration route. Millions of waterbirds depend on this coastal stopping point between breeding and wintering grounds.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1606/

co|A shark gathering far offshore|Around remote Malpelo island, observers have recorded groups of more than 200 hammerhead sharks and over 1,000 silky sharks. This little Colombian island sits about 506 km from the coast.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1216/

km|Island cities shaped by both family lines|The historic Comorian sultanate towns developed with matrilineal and matrilocal customs alongside patrilineal Islamic traditions. Their streets and buildings reflect centuries of Indian Ocean cultural exchange.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1768/

cr|A rainforest far out in the Pacific|Cocos Island lies about 550 km off Costa Rica. UNESCO identifies it as the tropical eastern Pacific’s only island with a tropical rainforest; underwater, it is famous for large ocean-going animals.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/820/

hr|A cathedral with 71 faces|The Cathedral of St James in Šibenik has a frieze of 71 sculpted faces of women, men and children. Its builders also constructed the cathedral entirely from stone.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/963/

cu|Plants that learned to live with toxic rock|Some rocks in Alejandro de Humboldt National Park are chemically hostile to plants. Adaptation to those conditions helped produce a remarkable variety of species found nowhere else.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/839/

cy|Plain outside, spectacular inside|The rural exteriors of some Troodos churches look modest. Inside, elaborate Byzantine and later murals cover the walls—a striking contrast preserved across ten listed monuments.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/351/

cz|A landscape designed like a garden|The Lednice-Valtice estate covers about 200 square kilometres. Its rulers reshaped whole stretches of countryside, combining castles and Baroque buildings with English-inspired romantic landscaping.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/763/

ci|A river that brings a different habitat|The Comoé River allows patches of rainforest to occur much farther north than expected. Its park mixes those forests with savannah vegetation in the same protected landscape.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/227/

cd|A rainforest reached by water|Salonga, described by UNESCO as Africa’s largest tropical rainforest reserve, is so isolated that access is by water. It protects animals such as bonobos and Congo peacocks.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/280/

dk|A prehistoric aquarium in the cliffs|The cliffs of western Limfjord preserve exceptionally detailed fossil fish, along with turtles, birds and insects. These remains reveal how life responded to a major warming episode in the early Eocene.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1758/

dm|A lake that boils|Dominica’s Morne Trois Pitons National Park contains a boiling lake, hot springs and dozens of steam vents. Its tropical forest grows across a remarkably active volcanic landscape.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/814/

do|A city used as a planning template|Santo Domingo’s colonial grid became a model for later towns across the Americas. UNESCO also records the city’s early cathedral, hospital, customs house and university as regional firsts.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/526/

ec|Three currents, one evolutionary laboratory|Three ocean currents meet around the Galápagos. Combined with volcanic activity and isolation, that setting helped produce the unusual wildlife that influenced Darwin after his 1835 visit.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1/

eg|Whales with legs—in the desert|Egypt’s Whale Valley preserves fossils of early whales during their transition from land to sea. Some show the stage when these animals were losing their hind limbs.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1186/

sv|A farming village frozen by a volcano|Joya de Cerén was buried by an eruption around 600 CE. Like Pompeii, its exceptional preservation offers a close look at ordinary lives—in this case a Central American farming community.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/675/

er|Modernist architecture high in Africa|Asmara sits more than 2,000 metres above sea level and preserves an extensive early-modernist cityscape. Cinemas, hotels and religious buildings reflect a major 1930s building programme under Italian colonial rule.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1550/

ee|A medieval trading city still readable today|Tallinn’s old town grew rich through the Hanseatic trading network. Its surviving merchants’ houses and public buildings let you trace that commercial world through the streets.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/822/

et|A goat with a very small world|The Walia ibex is found only in Ethiopia’s Simien Mountains. The same landscape has cliffs dropping around 1,500 metres and wildlife adapted to its dramatic high-altitude terrain.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/9/

fj|Fiji’s first colonial capital was not Suva|It was Levuka, a port town along the beach on Ovalau. Its layout grew around existing indigenous villages, whose residents continued to outnumber European settlers.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1399/

fi|An industrial time capsule|Verla preserves a rural paper-and-board mill settlement of a kind once widespread across northern Europe and North America. Only a handful of comparable settlements survived so completely.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/751/

fr|France has a penguin chapter|Remote French islands in the southern Indian Ocean support enormous colonies of king penguins. French geography reaches far beyond Europe into sub-Antarctic seas.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1603/

ga|Waterfalls with their own miniature worlds|Ivindo National Park’s rivers and waterfalls shelter highly localised aquatic plants. UNESCO notes that parts remain little studied and some fish species have yet to be formally described.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1653/

gm|A small island with a long historical reach|Kunta Kinteh Island sits in the River Gambia. Its remains record successive chapters of African–European contact, including the slave trade and its abolition.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/761/

ge|A monastery that was also an academy|Founded in 1106, Gelati was a major centre of science and education in medieval Georgia. Its academy made the monastery a place for scholarship as well as worship.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/710/

de|Ice Age people made music too|Caves in Germany’s Swabian Jura have yielded musical instruments as well as carved animals and jewellery. The finds date back roughly 33,000–43,000 years.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1527/

gh|An Atlantic archive built in stone|Ghana’s coastal forts and trading posts were built across more than 300 years, from 1482 to 1786. Their remains mark successive phases of Atlantic trade and European expansion.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/34/

gr|The gods had a real mountain address|Mount Olympus is a real Greek mountain landscape, not merely a mythical place. Ancient writers made it the home of the Olympian gods, while its steep terrain shelters varied habitats.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1719/

gt|A crossroads between civilizations|Tak’alik Ab’aj records about 1,700 years of history spanning the transition from Olmec to early Maya culture. Trade carried ideas through the site as well as goods.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1663/

gn|Tool-using chimpanzees and unusual toads|Mount Nimba shelters chimpanzees that use stones as tools and a toad that gives birth to live young. Its mountain habitats rise above the surrounding savannah.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/155/

gw|An island stopover for a huge bird migration|The Bijagós protected landscape supports over 870,000 migratory shorebirds. It is also part of the only active deltaic archipelago on Africa’s Atlantic coast.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1431/

ht|A fortress built after a revolution|Haiti’s Citadel and Sans Souci belong to the years after independence. UNESCO recognises these monuments as symbols of the freedom won by formerly enslaved people.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/180/

hn|Mountains that run down to the Caribbean|The Río Plátano reserve links mountainous rainforest to the Caribbean shore. Its landscape is also a long-standing home for indigenous communities, rather than an uninhabited wilderness.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/196/

hu|A school inside a thousand-year-old community|Benedictine monks settled at Pannonhalma in 996 and established Hungary’s first school. The abbey’s long educational tradition continues alongside its monastic life.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/758/

is|An island with a birth date|Surtsey emerged from volcanic eruptions between 1963 and 1967. Protected from ordinary human disturbance, it lets scientists watch plants and animals colonise brand-new land.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1267/

in|Bridges made from living roots|In Meghalaya, communities guide and weave the living roots of rubber fig trees across streams. Over time, the roots form usable bridges—a piece of infrastructure that is still alive.|https://whc.unesco.org/fr/listesindicatives/6606

id|From tropical sea to snowy mountains|Lorentz National Park spans environments from marine waters and wetlands to high mountain terrain shaped by glaciers. It is a startling reminder that Indonesia has an alpine world as well as tropical islands.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/955/

ir|A thousand-year-old brick skyscraper|Gonbad-e Qābus is a 53-metre tomb tower built in 1006. Its tapering cylinder and conical roof demonstrate sophisticated geometry using ordinary unglazed fired bricks.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1398/

iq|A wetland world in an arid country|Southern Iraq’s Ahwar is a vast inland delta of marshes in a very hot, dry region. Nearby are the remains of Ur, Uruk and Eridu, cities of ancient Mesopotamia.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1481/

ie|Stone-age art on a monumental scale|The Boyne Valley’s Newgrange, Knowth and Dowth form an exceptional concentration of prehistoric stone art. These monuments served social and ceremonial roles as well as burial functions.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/659/

il|Half a million years in four caves|The Mount Carmel caves preserve evidence spanning at least 500,000 years of human evolution. Finds include both Neanderthals and early modern humans within the same broad prehistoric cultural tradition.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1393/

it|A volcano with a very long written record|Mount Etna’s activity has been documented for at least 2,700 years. Its much longer geological record reaches back roughly half a million years.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1427/

jm|Mountains that became a refuge|Jamaica’s Blue and John Crow Mountains sheltered Taino people and later Maroon communities escaping slavery. Trails, settlements and forest knowledge helped communities resist colonial control.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1356/

jp|Wooden buildings from the seventh century|Some Buddhist buildings at Horyu-ji date to the late 600s or early 700s. They are among the world’s oldest surviving wooden structures—not stone ruins, but timber architecture.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/660/

jo|Monks who lived on towers|At Um er-Rasas, two surviving towers are associated with stylites: ascetic monks who isolated themselves on top of columns or towers. The site also contains elaborate mosaic floors.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1093/

kz|A grand building left unfinished|The Yasawi mausoleum was begun under Timur in 1389 and remained partly unfinished. Its builders tested architectural ideas later used in the empire’s great capital, Samarkand.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1103/

ke|A flamingo feeding destination|Kenya’s Rift Valley lakes are crucial feeding grounds for lesser flamingos. Bogoria, Nakuru and Elementaita form a linked lake system supporting extraordinary bird diversity.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1060/

ki|Mountains hidden under the Pacific|Kiribati’s Phoenix Islands protected area includes 14 known underwater seamounts, thought to be extinct volcanoes. Its ocean habitats cover over 400,000 square kilometres.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1325/

kg|A mountain home for fruit ancestors|The Western Tien-Shan is an important centre of origin for cultivated fruit crops. These mountain forests are part of the deeper story behind familiar fruit on a dinner table.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1490/

la|Two architectural worlds in one town|Luang Prabang blends traditional Lao buildings and urban patterns with French colonial architecture. The combination is preserved across a whole townscape, not just a single landmark.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/479/

lv|Survey markers that helped measure Earth|Latvia is on the Struve Geodetic Arc, a 2,820-km chain of survey points across ten countries. Nineteenth-century measurements along it helped establish Earth’s size and shape.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1187/

lb|Trees once prized for great buildings|Lebanon’s surviving cedar forests connect to an ancient building material traded and valued across the region. Nearby Qadisha’s monasteries cling to a dramatic mountain valley.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/850/

ls|A mountain kingdom with rock-art galleries|Lesotho shares the Maloti-Drakensberg landscape with South Africa. Its cliffs, caves and rock shelters preserve a remarkable concentration of paintings as well as highland wildlife.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/985/

ly|A desert city with streets under the houses|In Ghadamès, homes overhang covered alleys, creating sheltered passageways. Traditionally, supplies were kept below, families lived above, and women used the open rooftop terraces.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/362/

lt|A capital that transformed a provincial town|Kaunas served as Lithuania’s provisional capital between the world wars. That role triggered a wave of modernist public buildings, homes and urban planning in just two decades.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1661/

lu|A fortress repeatedly upgraded by its owners|Luxembourg’s strategic position made successive European powers reinforce its defences. Centuries of fortification ended with the dismantling of its walls beginning in 1867.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/699/

mg|An evolutionary experiment lasting millions of years|Madagascar’s long isolation helped its plants and animals evolve independently. Its eastern rainforests preserve part of that distinctive world, including rare lemurs.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1257/

mw|A mountain rising like an island|Mount Mulanje is an enormous inselberg—a mountain mass rising above the surrounding landscape. For local communities, its water, rocks and forests also belong to a sacred landscape.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1201/

my|A room hundreds of metres wide—underground|Sarawak Chamber in Gunung Mulu is about 600 metres long, 415 metres wide and 80 metres high. The surrounding cave network is home to millions of bats and swiftlets.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1013/

ml|A pyramid built from mud|The Tomb of Askia in Gao has a striking 17-metre pyramidal form. Built in 1495, it reflects the wealth of the Songhai Empire and the Sahel’s monumental earthen-building tradition.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1139/

mt|Hundreds of monuments in a tiny capital|UNESCO counts 320 monuments within Valletta’s 55 hectares. Malta’s capital packs an extraordinary amount of architectural history into a very small footprint.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/131/

mh|History beneath a lagoon|Bikini Atoll’s lagoon contains ships sunk during the 1946 nuclear tests. These underwater remains are part of a difficult history that also includes the displacement of the islanders.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1339/

mr|Desert dunes meet a bird-filled sea|At Banc d’Arguin, Sahara dunes sit beside shallow Atlantic waters, islands and coastal swamps. That abrupt meeting of desert and ocean creates a major wintering ground for migratory birds.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/506/

mu|A mountain that became a symbol of freedom|Escaped enslaved people sheltered on Le Morne’s wooded cliffs and in its caves. Their history gave this Mauritian mountain a meaning far beyond its dramatic outline.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1259/

mx|A forest made of cacti|The Tehuacán-Cuicatlán Valley has exceptionally dense forests of tall columnar cacti. It also preserves ancient canals, wells and dams that supported early agricultural settlements.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1534/

fm|A city built on artificial islets|Nan Madol is spread across more than 100 constructed islets off Pohnpei. Walls of basalt and coral boulders supported palaces, temples and homes built between roughly 1200 and 1500.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1503/

mn|A landscape that changes with climate cycles|Dauria’s alternating wet and dry periods create shifting habitats of grassland, forest, lakes and wetlands. These support migratory birds and the cross-border movements of Mongolian gazelles.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1448/

me|Glaciers above, rivers below|Durmitor’s dramatic landscape was carved by glaciers, then cut by rivers and underground streams. The Tara canyon is among Europe’s deepest gorges.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/100/

ma|Two very different city plans side by side|Rabat combines medieval walls and monuments with a large planned city built under the French protectorate. Its urban landscape lets you read two very different eras together.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1401/

mz|Coral reefs and savannah in one protected landscape|The Maputo–iSimangaliso coastal region crosses Mozambique and South Africa. Its habitats range from reefs and seagrass to freshwater lakes, mangroves and savannah.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/914/

mm|A whole landscape of sacred architecture|Bagan was a major imperial capital between the eleventh and thirteenth centuries. Its temples, stupas, monasteries and wall paintings preserve the scale of that Buddhist civilisation.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1588/

na|A desert that drinks fog|In the Namib Sand Sea, fog is the principal source of water. Animals adapted to it live among dunes made from material transported by rivers, ocean currents and wind.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1430/

np|Everest shares a home with red pandas|Sagarmatha National Park is famous for Everest, but it also protects rare wildlife such as red pandas and snow leopards. Its habitats extend through valleys, forests and high mountain terrain.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/120/

nl|Amsterdam’s canals were a city-building system|The canal ring was a planned expansion onto drained marshland. Concentric waterways and the spaces between them created new neighbourhoods and became an influential model of urban planning.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1349/

nz|A parrot that lives in the mountains|New Zealand’s kea is the world’s only alpine parrot. It lives in a landscape that also contains forests with trees more than 800 years old.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/551/

ni|A colonial town whose growth stopped|León Viejo never developed into a modern city on the same site. That makes its ruins an unusually clear record of an early Spanish settlement’s layout and society.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/613/

ne|A mountain refuge surrounded by the Sahara|The volcanic Aïr massif forms a pocket of different climate, plants and animals within the Ténéré desert. The reserve protects that contrast between mountain refuge and vast desert.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/573/

ng|A forest that is also an art landscape|The Osun-Osogbo Sacred Grove contains shrines, sculptures and sanctuaries among its trees and river bends. It preserves a Yoruba tradition of sacred forests once widespread around settlements.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1118/

kp|Ancient daily life painted on tomb walls|Some Koguryo tombs preserve murals showing a world that left few other remains. Painted tombs are rare among the thousands discovered across Korea and China.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1091/

mk|A lake with ancient survivors|Lake Ohrid shelters freshwater species with very old evolutionary lineages. Around its shores, archaeological evidence also records prehistoric settlements built on piles over the water.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/99/

no|A cliff that continues under the sea|The walls of Geirangerfjord and Nærøyfjord rise as much as 1,400 metres above the water and extend around 500 metres below sea level. The visible cliff is only part of the landscape.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1195/

om|A tree resin that powered trade routes|Frankincense helped connect Oman’s trees, desert caravan stops and ports to the wider ancient world. The Land of Frankincense sites preserve several parts of that trading system.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1010/

pk|A city remembered through its tombs|Thatta was the capital of three successive dynasties before Mughal rule. Its elaborate Makli necropolis preserves the artistic traditions of centuries of Sindh’s history.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/143/

pw|Seawater lakes cut off from the sea|Palau’s Rock Islands have an exceptional concentration of marine lakes: seawater enclosed by land. Their isolation has supported distinctive populations and continuing species discoveries.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1386/

pa|A natural bridge between continents|Darién links the ecosystems of North and South America. Within one national park are beaches, mangroves, swamps and both lowland and upland tropical forests.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/159/

pg|Agriculture developed here independently|At Kuk, people transformed highland wetlands into farmland over thousands of years. Archaeology points to an independent origin of agriculture, including early drainage ditches dug with wooden tools.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/887/

py|Ruins of a different kind of planned community|The Jesuit missions at Trinidad and Jesús preserve more than churches. They are remains of settlements built around religious, social and economic projects in the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/648/

pe|Tropical mountains with glaciers|Peru’s Cordillera Blanca is the world’s highest tropical mountain range. Huascarán National Park combines glaciers and glacial lakes with wildlife such as spectacled bears and Andean condors.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/333/

ph|A mountain with species of its own|Mount Hamiguitan shelters plants and animals found nowhere else. Its elevation changes create different habitats within one mountain ridge, including homes for the Philippine eagle and cockatoo.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1403/

pl|European bison have a forest stronghold|Białowieża Forest, shared with Belarus, protects the largest population of European bison. Its old forest includes both broadleaf trees and conifers.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/33/

pt|An aqueduct built to outlast a siege|Elvas’s defences include the Amoreira aqueduct, which helped supply the fortified town during long sieges. Its elaborate dry-ditch fortifications form an enormous interconnected defensive system.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1367/

qa|Before gas, there were pearls|Al Zubarah prospered through pearl diving and trade in the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Windblown desert sand later protected the abandoned town’s streets, homes and harbour remains.|https://whc.unesco.org/en/list/1402/
